---
title: "Choosing dictionary forms"
subtitle: "Compare teaching lemmas with a released pipeline"
description: "Learn how lemmas differ from stems and why lemmatizers built in different ways disagree on workforce text."
categories: [word processing, lemmatization, workforce research]
---

Stemming shortens the vocabulary but can produce strings such as `requir` and
`provid`. These strings help computers compare forms.
They are unsuitable as word labels in a public report.

The team wants readable labels for `is`, `provided`, and `classes`.
It compares model-selected dictionary forms with rule-based stems.
Model-selected forms can also be incorrect.

A **lemma** is a word's dictionary form.
**Lemmatization** chooses that form in context. This lesson compares a small
UDPipe teaching model with a released spaCy English pipeline.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching. Both models run locally.
The lesson downloads nothing during execution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- describe a lemma in plain language.
- compare a lemma with a Snowball stem.
- explain how tokenization changes the comparison set.
- describe the limits of a dictionary proxy.
- separate raw dictionary flags from broken-string counts.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load both lemmatizers

Both local lemmatizers use the same text file and table tools.
The code loads CSV and tokenization tools, the UDPipe model, and the spaCy
interface. It also loads SnowballC stemming and hunspell dictionary functions.
UDPipe receives one token per line. Its trained tagger returns lemmas through
model, dictionary, and guesser components.
spaCy receives raw text through the helper `use_project_spacy()`.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(tokenizers)
library(udpipe)
library(spacyr)
library(SnowballC)
library(hunspell)
source("R/use-spacy.R")

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

pipeline <- use_project_spacy()
spacy_info <- spacy_pipeline_version()
spacy_info_table <- tibble(
  item = names(spacy_info),
  value = unname(unlist(spacy_info))
)

udpipe_parser <- udpipe_load_model(
  "data/treebank/en_ewt-500-parser.udpipe"
)

vertical <- sentences$text |>
  tokenize_words(lowercase = FALSE, strip_punct = FALSE) |>
  map_chr(\(tokens) paste(tokens, collapse = "\n"))

udpipe_parsed <- udpipe_annotate(
  udpipe_parser,
  x = vertical,
  doc_id = sentences$sentence_id,
  tokenizer = "vertical",
  tagger = "default",
  parser = "default"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble()

spacy_text <- sentences$text
names(spacy_text) <- sentences$sentence_id

spacy_parsed <- spacy_parse(
  spacy_text,
  pos = TRUE,
  lemma = TRUE,
  entity = TRUE,
  dependency = TRUE,
  nounphrase = TRUE
) |>
  as_tibble()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  spacy_info_table,
  col.names = c("Pipeline field", "Value"),
  caption = "Local spaCy pipeline used by this lesson",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(pipeline$model, "en_core_web_sm"),
  identical(spacy_info$version, "3.8.0"),
  identical(spacy_info$license, "MIT"),
  identical(spacy_info$spacy, "3.8.7"),
  identical(nrow(udpipe_parsed), 178L),
  identical(nrow(spacy_parsed), 179L),
  identical(udpipe_parsed$lemma[udpipe_parsed$doc_id == "s001" & udpipe_parsed$token == "provided"], "provid"),
  identical(spacy_parsed$lemma[spacy_parsed$doc_id == "s001" & spacy_parsed$token == "provided"], "provide")
)
```

The local pipeline is `core_web_sm` version 3.8.0 under the MIT license, with
spaCy 3.8.7. UDPipe returns 178 tokens for the 28 text units.
spaCy returns 179 tokens. It splits `driver's` into `driver` and `'s`, while
the vertical tokenizer retains the whole word.
The comparison tables exclude `driver's` because spaCy has no matching
whole-word lemma.

## Compare lemmas with stems

The next table uses word types that appear in the Riverton sentences and that
both parsers emit as tokens. A stem and a lemma can agree, but they answer
different questions.

```{r}
known_to_hunspell <- \(words) map_lgl(hunspell(words), \(result) length(result) == 0L)

vocabulary_words <- sentences |>
  select(sentence_id, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  distinct(word) |>
  arrange(word)

udpipe_lookup <- udpipe_parsed |>
  filter(upos != "PUNCT") |>
  transmute(
    word = str_to_lower(token),
    udpipe_lemma = str_to_lower(lemma)
  ) |>
  group_by(word) |>
  summarise(udpipe_lemma = first(udpipe_lemma), .groups = "drop")

spacy_lookup <- spacy_parsed |>
  filter(pos != "PUNCT") |>
  transmute(
    word = str_to_lower(token),
    spacy_lemma = str_to_lower(lemma)
  ) |>
  group_by(word) |>
  summarise(spacy_lemma = first(spacy_lemma), .groups = "drop")

same_word_lemmas <- vocabulary_words |>
  left_join(udpipe_lookup, by = "word") |>
  left_join(spacy_lookup, by = "word")

comparison_words <- c(
  "is",
  "provided",
  "required",
  "classes",
  "shifts",
  "applicants",
  "training",
  "schedules",
  "paid",
  "pays"
)

lemma_stem_comparison <- same_word_lemmas |>
  filter(word %in% comparison_words) |>
  mutate(
    stem = wordStem(word, language = "en"),
    udpipe_known = known_to_hunspell(udpipe_lemma),
    spacy_known = known_to_hunspell(spacy_lemma)
  ) |>
  arrange(match(word, comparison_words))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  lemma_stem_comparison,
  col.names = c(
    "Word",
    "UDPipe lemma",
    "spaCy lemma",
    "Snowball stem",
    "UDPipe lemma known",
    "spaCy lemma known"
  ),
  caption = "Lemmas and stems for selected Riverton word types",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(vocabulary_words), 96L),
  identical(sum(is.na(same_word_lemmas$spacy_lemma)), 1L),
  identical(same_word_lemmas$word[is.na(same_word_lemmas$spacy_lemma)], "driver's"),
  identical(lemma_stem_comparison$udpipe_lemma[1:4], c("be", "provid", "requi", "classe")),
  identical(lemma_stem_comparison$spacy_lemma[1:4], c("be", "provide", "require", "class")),
  identical(lemma_stem_comparison$stem[1:4], c("is", "provid", "requir", "class")),
  identical(nrow(lemma_stem_comparison), 10L)
)
```

`is` shows why a lemma can be better than a stem. A stemmer leaves `is` alone,
while both parsers choose `be`. The sharper contrast is `provided`: the UDPipe
teaching model returns `provid`, while spaCy returns `provide`. For `classes`,
UDPipe returns `classe`, while spaCy returns `class`.

The simplified table omits context. A word type can receive different lemmas
in different sentences. The next check finds word types with multiple
lemmas from at least one tool.

```{r}
lemma_variation <- bind_rows(
  udpipe_parsed |>
    filter(upos != "PUNCT") |>
    transmute(system = "UDPipe", word = str_to_lower(token), lemma = str_to_lower(lemma)),
  spacy_parsed |>
    filter(pos != "PUNCT") |>
    transmute(system = "spaCy", word = str_to_lower(token), lemma = str_to_lower(lemma))
) |>
  group_by(system, word) |>
  summarise(
    distinct_lemmas = n_distinct(lemma),
    lemmas = paste(sort(unique(lemma)), collapse = ", "),
    occurrences = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(distinct_lemmas > 1L) |>
  arrange(system, word)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  lemma_variation,
  col.names = c("System", "Word type", "Distinct lemmas", "Lemmas seen", "Occurrences"),
  caption = "Word types whose lemmas vary across Riverton occurrences",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(lemma_variation$system, c("UDPipe", "UDPipe", "UDPipe", "spaCy")),
  identical(lemma_variation$word, c("evening", "paid", "skills", "skills")),
  identical(lemma_variation$distinct_lemmas, c(2L, 2L, 2L, 2L))
)
```

The systems differ in several ways.
The project trained the UDPipe teaching model on a 500-sentence excerpt.
spaCy provides a released English pipeline for general applications.
UDPipe combines its trained tagger with dictionary and guesser components.
spaCy's English lemmatizer uses lookup tables and part-of-speech rules.

The tools, tokenization, and training setup all differ.
This comparison therefore cannot isolate the effect of training size.

## Count dictionary flags

A simple check finds lemmas absent from hunspell's dictionary.
Dictionary absence does not prove that a string is not an English word.
The check cannot distinguish a valid missing entry, such as `riverton`, from
an error. It also misses incorrect lemmas that are dictionary words.
For example, it accepts `leave` for `left` in `the left column`.

The following analysis separates dictionary-coverage and case effects from
malformed strings. It does not measure overall lemma correctness.

```{r}
compared_word_lemmas <- same_word_lemmas |>
  filter(!is.na(udpipe_lemma), !is.na(spacy_lemma)) |>
  mutate(
    udpipe_known = known_to_hunspell(udpipe_lemma),
    spacy_known = known_to_hunspell(spacy_lemma),
    udpipe_flagged = !udpipe_known,
    spacy_flagged = !spacy_known,
    coverage_or_case_artifact = word %in% c("october", "riverton"),
    udpipe_broken_string = udpipe_flagged & !coverage_or_case_artifact,
    spacy_broken_string = spacy_flagged & !coverage_or_case_artifact
  )

lemma_quality <- tibble(
  system = c("UDPipe teaching model", "spaCy released pipeline"),
  word_types_compared = c(nrow(compared_word_lemmas), nrow(compared_word_lemmas)),
  raw_dictionary_flags = c(
    sum(compared_word_lemmas$udpipe_flagged),
    sum(compared_word_lemmas$spacy_flagged)
  ),
  coverage_or_case_artifacts = c(
    sum(compared_word_lemmas$udpipe_flagged & compared_word_lemmas$coverage_or_case_artifact),
    sum(compared_word_lemmas$spacy_flagged & compared_word_lemmas$coverage_or_case_artifact)
  ),
  broken_string_flags = c(
    sum(compared_word_lemmas$udpipe_broken_string),
    sum(compared_word_lemmas$spacy_broken_string)
  )
)

flagged_comparison <- compared_word_lemmas |>
  filter(udpipe_flagged | spacy_flagged) |>
  select(
    word,
    udpipe_lemma,
    spacy_lemma,
    udpipe_flagged,
    spacy_flagged,
    coverage_or_case_artifact,
    udpipe_broken_string,
    spacy_broken_string
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  lemma_quality,
  col.names = c(
    "System",
    "Word types compared",
    "Raw dictionary flags",
    "Coverage or case artifacts",
    "Broken-string flags"
  ),
  caption = "Dictionary proxy counts for lemmas on the same Riverton word types",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  flagged_comparison,
  col.names = c(
    "Word",
    "UDPipe lemma",
    "spaCy lemma",
    "UDPipe flagged",
    "spaCy flagged",
    "Coverage or case artifact",
    "UDPipe broken string",
    "spaCy broken string"
  ),
  caption = "Where either model's lemma is flagged by hunspell",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(compared_word_lemmas), 95L),
  identical(lemma_quality$raw_dictionary_flags, c(8L, 2L)),
  identical(lemma_quality$coverage_or_case_artifacts, c(2L, 2L)),
  identical(lemma_quality$broken_string_flags, c(6L, 0L)),
  identical(
    flagged_comparison$word,
    c("classes", "diploma", "includes", "need", "october", "provided", "required", "riverton")
  ),
  identical(
    flagged_comparison$udpipe_lemma,
    c("classe", "diploman", "includ", "ne", "october", "provid", "requi", "riverton")
  ),
  identical(flagged_comparison$spacy_flagged, c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE))
)
```

Both parsers provide lemmas for 95 word types.
Hunspell flags 8 UDPipe lemmas and 2 spaCy lemmas.
Both systems have flags for `riverton` and `october`, which are not model
errors. The first is a fictional place name.
The second results from lowercasing before dictionary lookup.
spaCy originally returned `October`, which hunspell recognizes.

Excluding those cases, UDPipe produced six malformed strings:
`classe`, `diploman`, `includ`, `ne`, `provid`, and `requi`.
spaCy produced none. Six word types are a small count from 28 text units of
one type.

## Decide when the cost is justified

For a public table, an examined lemma is usually safer than a Snowball stem.
`is` and `are` can group under `be`, and `provided` can become `provide` rather
than `provid`.

Stemming requires less computation and often suffices for approximate internal
matching. Strings such as `requir` and `schedul` are unsuitable for display
as words. Correct lemmas provide readable labels.
The UDPipe `provid` example shows that lemma columns still need checks.

```{r}
final_check <- tibble(
  model = c("UDPipe", "spaCy"),
  provided_lemma = c(
    lemma_stem_comparison$udpipe_lemma[lemma_stem_comparison$word == "provided"],
    lemma_stem_comparison$spacy_lemma[lemma_stem_comparison$word == "provided"]
  )
)

invisible(suppressMessages(spacy_finalize()))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  final_check,
  col.names = c("Model", "Lemma for provided"),
  caption = "A final check on the clearest contrast",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(final_check$provided_lemma, c("provid", "provide")),
  identical(spacy_info$version, "3.8.0"),
  identical(spacy_info$spacy, "3.8.7")
)
```

## What to remember

- A lemma is a dictionary form chosen for a word in context.
- A stem is a rule-based comparison string.
- Tokenizers changed the comparison: `driver's` has no spaCy word-type match.
- The dictionary screen flags unknown strings, not lemma correctness.
- Raw hunspell flags are 8 for UDPipe and 2 for spaCy on 95 word types.
- Excluding coverage and case artifacts, the broken-string count is 6 for UDPipe
  and 0 for spaCy.

Examine malformed or unexpected lemmas before using them to group public
labels. This comparison finds six small-model outputs for further checks.
It does not establish a causal effect of training size.
